title: The Fall of the USSR, Pt I
summary: Part one of a two-part series on the fall of the Soviet Union (USSR). Josh and Chuck explain how Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms of perestroika (economic restructuring) and glasnost (transparency) unexpectedly unraveled Soviet control. They cover the inherited planned economy and its shortages, the costs of Afghanistan and Chernobyl, the press exposing Soviet social ills, the renunciation of the Brezhnev Doctrine, and the 1989 collapse of communist satellite states including Poland's Solidarity election win and Romania's revolution and the Ceausescus' execution. The episode closes as Baltic and Ukrainian republics begin seceding in 1990 and 1991, with Russia's place in the union in question. Ends with a cliffhanger to part two; no listener mail.

entities.name: Communist Party of the Soviet Union

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the two-part series on the USSR's sudden collapse and note the end of the Cold War.

segments.title: Gorbachev and perestroika
segments.summary: Gorbachev's reforms of perestroika and glasnost are introduced as a top-down effort; Josh argues he was surprised by the consequences. The Soviet economy under stagnation is described.

segments.title: The inherited Soviet planned economy
segments.summary: The ruble was not recognized outside the Eastern Bloc, the state set production and prices, and shortages and waste followed.

segments.title: Afghanistan and Chernobyl costs
segments.summary: Chuck explains that military spending, the Afghanistan war, and the Chernobyl cleanup strained Soviet finances.

segments.title: Chernobyl miniseries aside
segments.summary: Brief discussion of the Chernobyl miniseries with Jared Harris.

segments.title: Perestroika reforms: joint ventures and private business
segments.summary: Reforms allowed foreign joint ventures, handing some state enterprises to worker collectives, and producing beyond quotas. The reforms caused problems: republics withheld taxes, ministers looted industry, and the ruble stayed controlled.

segments.title: Glasnost and state censorship
segments.summary: Glasnost relaxed state censorship after the Chernobyl cover-up, exposing famine, the gulags, and other social ills in the media.

segments.title: Gorbachev's motives and the nomenklatura
segments.summary: Gorbachev's openness is described as sincere and politically calculated; he came from the Nomenklatura elite and may have been out of touch.

segments.title: Press reaction and national identity
segments.summary: The press began reporting Soviet ills; the exposure shook Soviet identity. Ancient Albanian-Serb hostilities re-emerged, leading to Balkan fighting in the 1990s.

segments.title: Western culture and Brezhnev Doctrine renounced
segments.summary: Western movies and Billy Joel's Soviet concerts opened eyes to Western culture. Gorbachev renounced the Brezhnev Doctrine, removing the military backing for satellite states.

segments.title: Satellite states and the Iron Curtain
segments.summary: Distinction between the fifteen Soviet republics and the satellite states; freedom of travel let East Germans leave for Austria via Budapest.

segments.title: Polish Solidarity election of 1989
segments.summary: Solidarity, a former trade union turned party, was allowed to run; it won the allotted seats and 99 of 100 Senate seats. Poland became non-communist; a joke about Polish stereotypes follows.

segments.title: 1989 revolutions and Romania
segments.summary: The Berlin Wall fell and Germany reunified; Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, and others changed government. Romania's revolution was bloody; Ceausescu ordered fire on protesters, the military defected, and the couple were tried and executed. Rumors about dogs and the dog-related jokes are discussed.

segments.title: Romanian dog rumors and Dennis Miller joke
segments.summary: The rumor that the Ceausescus were fed to dogs is described as unconfirmed; the hosts recall a Dennis Miller joke.

segments.title: Gorbachev's non-intervention and power devolution
segments.summary: Gorbachev stayed out of the crumbling bloc, devolved power, and acted unilaterally as head of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.

segments.title: Congress of People's Deputies and republic secessions
segments.summary: Gorbachev created a Congress of People's Deputies and an presidency in March 1990, dissolved the Communist Party's grip, and held elections. Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, Georgia, and Armenia moved to secede; Ukraine's referendum showed about 90 percent support for independence.

segments.title: Putin, Ukraine, and Russia's role
segments.summary: Putin reportedly views the breakup as illegitimate; Russia was the most powerful republic, and the hosts raise questions about what comes next.

segments.title: Closing and part two tease
segments.summary: Hosts end part one, skip listener mail per tradition, and tease part two on the dissolution.
